 IRS issues fresh warning to US taxpayers: ‘Sensitive’ data now at risk. Act before mid-November to protect your refund
 Jing Pan 2026년 10월 24일 토 오후 12:15 UTC 0 This article adheres to strict editorial standards. Some or all links may be monetized. 
 For Americans counting on a tax refund to pay down debt, rebuild savings or catch up on bills, having someone else file a fraudulent return in their name could turn a financial lifeline into a paperwork nightmare.
 The IRS is urging taxpayers to take steps now to protect their personal information — including one some taxpayers should take before an essential mid-November deadline.

 In an Oct. 22 release (1), the agency advised Americans to safeguard their IRS online account credentials and obtain an Identity Protection PIN to help prevent criminals from misusing their identities.
 “Protecting sensitive financial information is essential to preventing unauthorized users from accessing confidential tax information and IRS online services,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano.
 He added that those precautions can help taxpayers “protect themselves from bad actors.”
 Tax-related identity theft occurs when a criminal uses your Social Security number to submit a false return claiming a fraudulent refund. According to the IRS, your tax account is particularly vulnerable (2) when stolen information includes both your Social Security number and financial details, such as wages.
 And resolving a suspicious return can stand between you and your money.
 The IRS says (3) its Taxpayer Protection Program may send a letter asking you to verify your identity and return information. Until you respond, the agency cannot process the return or issue the refund.
 Take this step before mid-November
 The IRS offers a free tool to help protect you: an Identity Protection PIN, or IP PIN.
 This six-digit number helps the agency confirm your identity and prevent someone else from filing a federal return using your Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number.
 You can request one from the IRS (4) even if you aren’t required to file a return. For taxpayers planning to file early in 2027, the IRS recommends acting before its online PIN system becomes unavailable for annual maintenance in mid-November. It generally becomes available again in mid-January.
 An important detail: the number changes annually. Online participants continuing into 2027 will need to retrieve their new PIN for that year. Keep it secure and enter the correct number when filing to avoid a rejected electronic return or delayed paper return.
 Your tax refund isn’t the only money “bad actors” may be after. According to the Federal Trade Commission (5), consumers reported losing about $16 billion to fraud in 2025. The FTC notes that this number is likely a lowball, as most fraud goes unreported to the government.
 You can add another layer of protection by keeping a closer watch on your identity and where your money is going.

 Make your identity harder to steal
 Your personal information has value far beyond tax season. An unfamiliar credit application or a new account you never opened could signal that someone is trying to put your identity to work for themselves.
 If you want some added peace of mind, platforms like Aura offer a way to safeguard your personal information.
 The AI-powered service removes your personal data from Google search results, people-search sites and brokers that sell your data to advertisers. Aura can even scan the dark web and data breach sources for your credentials and alert you to any leaks of your data.
 Aura also monitors spending patterns so you always know when a suspicious transaction pops up, and if identity theft does happen, their $1 million insurance protection covers eligible losses and fees.
 You could even save up to 68% if you sign up today — and Aura even offers a risk-free, 60-day money-back guarantee .
 Keep a close eye on every dollar
 Protecting your money also means knowing what’s leaving your accounts. Between automatic payments, everyday purchases and recurring subscriptions, it’s easy for an unfamiliar transaction — or a service you stopped using months ago — to slip past unnoticed.
 A quick daily check-in of your accounts can show you exactly where your money is going.
 An app like Rocket Money can easily flag recurring subscriptions, upcoming bills and unusual charges by pulling in transactions from all your linked accounts.
 This can help you cut unnecessary costs, and then you can manually redirect savings straight into your retirement fund. No spreadsheets, no guesswork, no stress. Small habits like this can make a big difference over time.

Free features include subscription tracking, bill reminders and budgeting basics, while premium features — like automated savings, net worth tracking, customizable dashboards and more — make it easier to stay on top of your retirement contributions and overall financial goals.
